children: By Purvi Agarwal

Canada's benchmark index edged lower on Tuesday, trading near four-week lows, as rising bond yields and declines in precious metal prices dampened risk appetite, while an uptick in oil prices kept broader declines in check.
The S&P/TSX Composite Index
Global bond yields climbed to multi-month highs as renewed hostilities in the Middle East lifted oil prices, prompting markets to reassess expectations of rate hikes by central banks.
Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasury
bonds and the Canadian 10-year note (CA10YT=RR) rose to 4.776% and 3.758%, respectively, marking the highest levels for both since early 2025.
The surge in yields weighed on metal prices, with gold and silver both down more than 2% each. The materials sector
that houses Canadian miners lost 2.8%.
Barrick Mining
lost 2.5%, NovaGold Resources
was down 4.5%, while Equinox Gold
shed 4.2%.
Investors flocked to sectors considered traditionally defensive, with healthcare
and consumer staples (.GSPTTCS) adding 0.8% and 1.2%, respectively.
Rising oil prices lifted energy stocks
1.5%, giving the index a boost.

"Bond yields rising is not a good thing, you couple that with higher oil prices — good for energy companies — but not good for inflation... Today is glass half empty versus half full," said Allan Small, senior investment advisor for Allan Small Financial Group with iA Private Wealth.
The Bank of Canada is expected to announce its monetary policy decision on Wednesday, with markets largely expecting rates to remain unchanged.
Employment reports in the U.S. and at home, due later in the week, could influence expectations of how central banks will approach policy going ahead.
The TSX marked its fifth month of gains on Monday, as miners posted a stellar rally on the back of rising metal prices.
Canada's manufacturing sector expanded for a fifth straight month in August, data from S&P Global showed.
